intro.why: Parsing turns a flat string into a structure that says who did what to whom. Constituency parsing introduces grammars, dynamic programming over spans (CKY), and probabilistic disambiguation, ideas that recur in dependency parsing (M10), semantic parsing and structured prediction generally.
prereq: Session M6–M7 (POS tags, dynamic programming with Viterbi)

symbols: best probability of A spanning words i..j

sections.title: Structural ambiguity and the growth of parses
sections.plain: The same words can be grouped in several valid ways, and the number of groupings grows explosively.
sections.body:
"I saw the man with the telescope": did I use the telescope, or did the man have it? Both trees are grammatical; the difference is where the prepositional phrase (PP) attaches, to the verb phrase or to the noun phrase. This is structural ambiguity (as opposed to lexical ambiguity of single words).

Each additional PP can attach to more places, and the number of parses follows the Catalan numbers:

  • "I saw the man with the telescope." → 2
  • "… the man on the hill with the telescope." → 5
  • "… on the hill in Texas with the telescope." → 14
  • "… on the hill in Texas with the telescope at noon on Monday." → 132

So a parser needs (1) a grammar defining the valid structures, (2) an efficient way to find them without enumerating, and (3) a way to choose the most plausible one.

sections.title: Context-free grammars and phrase structure
sections.plain: A grammar is a set of rewrite rules that build sentences from phrases and phrases from words.
sections.body:
A context-free grammar is G = (N, Σ, R, S): non-terminals N (S, NP, VP, PP, Det…), terminals Σ (the words), rules R of the form A → β (one non-terminal rewritten as a sequence), and start symbol S. "Context-free" means a rule applies to A regardless of what surrounds it.

Language is organised into phrases (constituents) named after their head: NP headed by a noun ("the large can", "NLP"), VP by a verb ("hold the water", "is interesting"), PP by a preposition ("with the telescope"). A parse tree for "NLP is very interesting":

(S (NP (N NLP)) (VP (V is) (AdjP (Adv very) (Adj interesting))))

Constituency tests: a constituent can be moved, replaced by a pronoun, or used as an answer ("What did you see? The man with the telescope.").

sections.title: Top-down vs bottom-up parsing
sections.plain: Start from the sentence symbol and expand, or start from the words and combine; both waste effort when they backtrack.
sections.body:
Top-down (the architect): start from S, expand rules (S → NP VP, NP → Det N…) until the leaves match the words. It never builds structures that can't be part of a sentence, but it wastes time on expansions that don't match the actual words, and left-recursive rules (NP → NP PP) can loop forever.

Bottom-up (the builder): start from the words, find categories for them, and combine adjacent constituents with rules until an S covers everything. It only builds what the words support, but it builds sub-structures that never fit into a full sentence (e.g. NP over the verb "barks").

Both, implemented naively with backtracking, throw away work after a wrong guess and re-parse the same sub-phrases again and again; on ambiguous sentences that duplicate work grows exponentially.

sections.title: Chart parsing
sections.plain: Store every completed piece so it is never built twice.
sections.body:
A chart parser applies dynamic programming: once it proves that "the large can" (words 0–3) is an NP, it records NP(0–3) in the chart and never re-derives it. A bottom-up chart parser keeps:

  1. Key: the constituent currently being processed.
  2. Chart: completed constituents with their spans.
  3. Agenda: newly found constituents not yet processed.
  4. Active arcs: partially matched rules waiting for more pieces.

Dotted rules track progress: NP → • ART ADJ N (nothing found), NP → ART • ADJ N (article found), NP → ART ADJ N • (complete; goes to the agenda). When a key of category C arrives, every arc waiting for C right after its dot advances. CKY and the Earley algorithm are both chart parsers; with charts, all parses of a sentence can be represented in polynomial (O(n³)) time and space, even when their number is exponential.

sections.title: Probabilistic CFGs
sections.plain: Give every rule a probability; a tree's probability is the product of its rules; pick the most probable tree.
sections.body:
A PCFG attaches a conditional probability to each rule, P(A → β) = P(β | A), with $\sum_\beta P(A\to\beta) = 1$ for every A. Probabilities are estimated from a treebank by counting: $P(A\to\beta) = C(A\to\beta)/C(A)$. The probability of a tree is the product of the rules used: $P(T) = \prod_i P(r_i)$.

Worked: "astronomers saw stars with ears". Rules: S → NP VP 1.0; NP → NP PP 0.4; PP → P NP 1.0; VP → V NP 0.7; VP → VP PP 0.3; P → with 1.0; V → saw 1.0; NP → astronomers 0.1 | ears 0.18 | saw 0.04 | stars 0.18 | telescope 0.1.

  • T1 (PP attached to VP: seeing with ears): 1.0 × 0.1 × 0.3 × 0.7 × 1.0 × 0.18 × 1.0 × 1.0 × 0.18 = 0.0006804.
  • T2 (PP attached to NP: stars that have ears): 1.0 × 0.1 × 0.7 × 1.0 × 0.4 × 0.18 × 1.0 × 1.0 × 0.18 = 0.0009072.

T2 is preferred. (Funny, but it's what these statistics say: a PCFG knows nothing about ears or stars.)

sections.title: Chomsky normal form and CKY
sections.plain: Convert the grammar to binary rules, then fill a triangular table of spans from short to long.
sections.body:
Chomsky normal form allows only A → B C and A → a. Conversions: replace terminals inside longer rules (NP → the Nominal ⇒ Det → the, NP → Det Nominal); remove unit productions (NP → Nominal, Nominal → Noun PP ⇒ NP → Noun PP); binarise long rules (NP → Det Noun PP ⇒ NP → Det X, X → Noun PP). The language is unchanged; trees can be converted back.

Probabilistic CKY (Cocke–Kasami–Younger) fills π[i, j, A] = best probability that A spans words i..j:

$$\pi[i,j,A] = \max_{A\to BC,\ i

with backpointers, for spans of length 1, 2, …, n; the answer is π[0, n, S]. Cost O(n³·|G|). Example: "The flight includes a meal": NP over "the flight" = P(NP → Det N) × P(Det) × P(N) = 0.3 × 0.4 × 0.02 = 0.0024. On the astronomers sentence, the span-4 cell compares VP → V NP (0.009072) with VP → VP PP (0.006804) and keeps the max, giving P(S) = 0.0009072.

sections.title: Weaknesses of PCFGs
sections.plain: Rule probabilities ignore the actual words and where in the tree a rule is used.
sections.body:
No lexicalisation: rules see only categories. VP → V NP NP gets the same probability for "give him a book" (fine) and "sleep him a book" (impossible); PP attachment in "eat pizza with a fork" vs "with anchovies" can't be resolved from tags alone. Lexicalised PCFGs annotate each node with its head word (VP(give) → V(give) NP NP), at the cost of sparsity.

No structural context: an NP expands to a pronoun much more often as a subject than as an object, but a PCFG has one P(NP → PRP). Fixes include parent annotation (NP^S vs NP^VP) and other state splitting.

Modern constituency parsers use neural span scorers (often on top of BERT-like encoders) with CKY-style decoding, reaching F1 above 95 on standard English benchmarks.

sections.title: PARSEVAL evaluation
sections.plain: Compare predicted labelled brackets with the gold treebank's.
sections.body:
Represent each tree as a set of labelled constituents (label, start, end), e.g. NP(0:2). Then

$$LP = \frac{\#\text{correct predicted}}{\#\text{predicted}},\qquad LR = \frac{\#\text{correct predicted}}{\#\text{gold}},\qquad F_1 = \frac{2\,LP\,LR}{LP + LR}$$

Worked: if the gold tree for the astronomers sentence is the VP-attachment one {S(0,5), VP(1,5), VP(1,3), PP(3,5)} and the parser outputs {S(0,5), VP(1,5), NP(2,5), PP(3,5)}, then 3 of 4 match: LP = LR = F1 = 0.75.

Why both matter: a parser that guesses 100 brackets for a short sentence may include all 6 gold ones (recall 100%) but its precision is 6% (F1 ≈ 0.11). Also report exact-match (whole tree correct) and, for downstream use, dependency accuracy after conversion.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Inside algorithm: CKY with sum instead of max gives the total sentence probability P(w), used to train PCFGs without trees (inside–outside EM).
  • Garden paths ("The horse raced past the barn fell") show humans parse incrementally and can be misled, unlike CKY, which keeps all analyses.
  • Treebanks: the Penn Treebank (~40k annotated newspaper sentences) made statistical parsing possible.
  • Constituency vs dependency: trees can be converted (via head rules) into dependencies (M10).

code.title: Catalan growth, PCFG trees and CNF conversion
code.explain: Prints 2, 5, 14, 42, 132 parses for 1–5 PPs, checks that each non-terminal's rule probabilities sum to 1, computes P(T1) = 0.0006804 and P(T2) = 0.0009072, and converts three rules into Chomsky normal form.
mistakes: Forgetting lexical rules in the tree product.
Leaving unit productions in a 'CNF' grammar.
code.notes: The CNF converter handles only the three patterns shown.
code.code:
"""Growth of PP-attachment ambiguity, PCFG tree probabilities, and CNF conversion."""
from math import comb, prod

# 1. Catalan numbers: n prepositional phrases -> C(n+1) bracketings
catalan = lambda n: comb(2 * n, n) // (n + 1)
for pps in range(1, 6):
    print(f"{pps} PP(s): {catalan(pps + 1)} parses")

# 2. PCFG: 'astronomers saw stars with ears'
R = {"S->NP VP": 1.0, "NP->NP PP": 0.4, "PP->P NP": 1.0, "VP->V NP": 0.7, "VP->VP PP": 0.3,
     "P->with": 1.0, "V->saw": 1.0, "NP->astronomers": 0.1, "NP->ears": 0.18, "NP->saw": 0.04,
     "NP->stars": 0.18, "NP->telescope": 0.1}
# each non-terminal's expansions sum to 1
for lhs in ["NP", "VP", "S", "PP"]:
    print(f"sum of P({lhs} -> ...) = {sum(p for r, p in R.items() if r.startswith(lhs + '->')):.2f}")
T1 = ["S->NP VP", "NP->astronomers", "VP->VP PP", "VP->V NP", "V->saw", "NP->stars", "PP->P NP", "P->with", "NP->ears"]
T2 = ["S->NP VP", "NP->astronomers", "VP->V NP", "V->saw", "NP->NP PP", "NP->stars", "PP->P NP", "P->with", "NP->ears"]
p1, p2 = prod(R[r] for r in T1), prod(R[r] for r in T2)
print(f"T1 (PP attached to VP: saw ... with ears) = {p1:.7f}")
print(f"T2 (PP attached to NP: stars with ears)   = {p2:.7f}  -> choose {'T2' if p2 > p1 else 'T1'}")

# 3. Converting rules to Chomsky normal form
rules = [("NP", ["the", "Nominal"]), ("NP", ["Det", "Noun", "PP"]), ("S", ["Aux", "NP", "VP", "PP"])]
def to_cnf(lhs, rhs, k=[0]):
    out = []
    rhs = [f"T_{w}" if w.islower() else w for w in rhs]          # terminals inside longer rules
    for w in rhs:
        if w.startswith("T_"): out.append((w, [w[2:]]))
    while len(rhs) > 2:                                             # binarise long rules
        k[0] += 1; new = f"X{k[0]}"
        out.append((new, rhs[-2:])); rhs = rhs[:-2] + [new]
    out.append((lhs, rhs))
    return out
for lhs, rhs in rules:
    print(f"{lhs} -> {' '.join(rhs)}   ==>   " + "; ".join(f"{a} -> {' '.join(b)}" for a, b in to_cnf(lhs, rhs)))
